questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What time was the last bus supposed to arrive?
questions.hint: Look in paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: “The timetable said the last bus would come at 6:15.”

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How is Amira feeling at the start of the story?
questions.hint: Look at how she holds her violin case and checks her watch.
questions.explanation: She clutches her case and checks her watch again and again — signs of worry.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 5, the headlights “swam out of the grey”. What does this suggest?
options: The bus had driven into the sea
The lights appeared slowly and blurrily through the rain
The headlights were moving very fast
questions.hint: Think about how things look through heavy rain.
questions.explanation: “Swam” suggests the lights drifted into view gradually and blurrily, as if through water.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why does the writer end the story with the empty shelter and the puddle?
options: To show that it had stopped raining
To leave a mysterious feeling — perhaps the old man was not an ordinary person
questions.hint: What is unusual about the ending?
questions.explanation: The man vanishes, leaving only a puddle, which creates mystery and makes the reader wonder who he was.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, which word could replace “clutching” without changing the meaning?
questions.hint: What do you do with something you are afraid to lose?
questions.explanation: “Clutching” means holding tightly — “gripping”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what does a camel’s hump store?

mistakes.2: The text says this is a popular belief that is wrong

questions.hint: Read paragraph 2 carefully — it corrects a common belief.
questions.explanation: “It stores fat, which the camel can use for energy.”

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why are camels called “ships of the desert”?
options: Because they were carried on ships
Like ships at sea, they carry people and goods across huge empty areas
questions.hint: Paragraph 1 explains the comparison.
questions.explanation: The metaphor compares crossing a desert to a ship crossing an ocean.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which detail best shows that camels are adapted to sandstorms?
options: They have been used for hundreds of years
They can drink 100 litres of water
questions.hint: Which feature helps when sand is blowing?
questions.explanation: Closing their nostrils keeps sand out during a sandstorm.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To introduce a new fact about camels
To give instructions for riding a camel
To tell a story about a camel
To sum up the main idea and speak directly to the reader
questions.hint: Is there new information, or a conclusion?
questions.explanation: It concludes the text by addressing the reader (“you”) and summarising that every feature helps survival.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is an adverb in this sentence? “The cat crept silently across the garden.”
questions.hint: Adverbs often tell us how something is done.
questions.explanation: “Silently” tells us how the cat crept — it is an adverb.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
options: The ball flew over the fence.
The window was broken by the ball.
questions.hint: In the passive, the thing that the action happens to comes first.
questions.explanation: “The window was broken by the ball” — the window (receiver of the action) is the subject.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
questions.hint: Apostrophes show possession or missing letters — not plurals.
questions.explanation: “The dog’s bowl” shows the bowl belongs to one dog.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.hint: The question mark goes inside the speech marks.
questions.explanation: Spoken words, including their punctuation, go inside the speech marks.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does the prefix “mis-” mean in “misunderstand” and “misbehave”?
questions.hint: Misbehave means to behave …
questions.explanation: “Mis-” means wrongly or badly.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which is the best way to join these sentences? “It was raining. We played inside.”
options: Because it was raining, we played inside.
It was raining but we played inside.
We played inside, it was raining.
It was raining, we played inside.

mistakes.3: A comma alone cannot join two sentences (comma splice)
mistakes.1: “But” shows contrast, which does not fit here

questions.hint: Show the reason for the action.
questions.explanation: “Because” shows the cause; the subordinate clause is followed by a comma.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence has been edited correctly? Original: “me and him goes to the park every saturday”
options: He and I go to the park every Saturday.
Him and I goes to the park every saturday.
He and me goes to the park every Saturday.
Me and him go to the park every Saturday.
questions.hint: Check pronouns, verb agreement and capital letters.
questions.explanation: “He and I” are subject pronouns, “go” agrees with a plural subject, and days of the week need capitals.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is a conjunction in this sentence? “I wanted to go out, although it was cold.”
questions.hint: A conjunction joins clauses.
questions.explanation: “Although” joins the two clauses.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why are solitary bees finding it harder to nest?
options: Gardens are being paved over and old walls repaired
They cannot find any flowers at all
They prefer to live in hives now
questions.hint: Paragraph 1, last sentence.
questions.explanation: The text says gardens are paved over and old walls are repaired, removing nesting places.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which materials does paragraph 2 say can be used to make the tubes? Select all that apply.
questions.hint: Paragraph 2 lists them. Select all that are mentioned.
questions.explanation: Bamboo canes, paper straws and holes drilled into wood are all mentioned.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Where should a bee hotel be placed? Choose the answer that matches paragraph 3.
options: Facing the evening sun, close to the ground
Anywhere, as long as it looks attractive
In a shady corner on the ground
Facing the morning sun, at least one metre high, sheltered from rain
questions.hint: Paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: It should face the morning sun, be at least 1 m above the ground and protected from heavy rain.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What can you infer from the fact that more than half of the tubes at Rivermouth were sealed?
options: The pupils sealed the tubes themselves
Many bees used the hotels to lay eggs
questions.hint: Who seals the tubes, according to paragraph 2?
questions.explanation: Bees seal a tube after laying an egg, so sealed tubes show the hotels were used.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does the comparison “like a block of flats in the middle of a desert” suggest?
options: A bee hotel is useless if there is no food nearby
Bee hotels should be built in deserts
Bees like to live in tall buildings
questions.hint: What would be the problem with flats in a desert?
questions.explanation: The simile suggests that, like people with no food or water around them, bees cannot survive in a hotel without flowers nearby.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why has the writer included the quotation from Tomas in paragraph 4?
options: To give a real example that shows bee hotels can work
To introduce a story about Tomas
To explain how to drill holes
To argue that bee hotels are dangerous
questions.hint: How does it support the main idea?
questions.explanation: A real example with a quotation makes the information more convincing and relatable.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 5, what does “caution” mean?
questions.hint: Scientists are pointing out a problem.
questions.explanation: To caution is to warn.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of this text?
options: To entertain readers with a story about bees
To instruct readers how to look after a hive
To persuade readers to buy honey
To inform readers about bee hotels and why they help
questions.hint: What does the text mostly do?
questions.explanation: It is an information text explaining what bee hotels are and how they help solitary bees.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What was Jonah doing when the storm began?
options: Pulling in the last lobster pot
questions.hint: Paragraph 1.
questions.explanation: He had just pulled the last lobster pot aboard.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: The sky “had turned the colour of a bruise”. What does this description suggest?
options: The sky was dark purple and threatening
The sky was bright and sunny
questions.hint: What colour is a bruise, and how does it make you feel?
questions.explanation: Bruises are dark purple-grey, so the sky was dark and menacing, hinting at danger.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which phrase from paragraph 2 is a simile?

mistakes.3: That is personification, not a simile

questions.hint: A simile compares using “like” or “as”.
questions.explanation: “Slapped the side of the little boat like an angry hand” uses “like” to compare.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How did Jonah know the light came from his grandmother?
options: It was the only house on the coast
It flashed the same pattern she had used every night for years
questions.hint: Paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: The light flashed a pattern — once, twice, pause, once — that his grandmother had used for eleven years.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why does the grandmother “not say a word” at the end?
options: She is angry and refuses to talk
She cannot hear because of the storm
She is too relieved and emotional to speak — her actions show her love
questions.hint: What does she do instead of speaking?
questions.explanation: She wraps him in her coat — her actions show relief and love more strongly than words.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How does the writer build tension in paragraph 2?
options: A long description of the harbour
Short sentences and a sputtering engine create a sense of danger
questions.hint: Look at sentence lengths and what goes wrong.
questions.explanation: Short sentences (“Rain stung his face.”) and the failing engine make the danger feel immediate.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, what does “gloom” mean?
questions.hint: Think about the weather and time of day.
questions.explanation: “Gloom” means darkness or dim light.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which technique is used in “the shutters yawn”?
questions.hint: Can shutters really yawn?
questions.explanation: Giving shutters a human action (yawning) is personification.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why does the poet say the baker’s window “glows like gold”?
options: To show the bread is expensive
To show it looks warm, bright and inviting in the grey morning
Because the window is made of gold
questions.hint: Compare it with the “grey” of the city.
questions.explanation: The simile contrasts warm golden light with the grey dawn, making the bakery seem inviting.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How does the mood change in the final verse?
options: From quiet and sleepy to busy and fast
questions.hint: Compare verse 1 with verse 3.
questions.explanation: The first verses are calm and slow; the final verse is full of racing footsteps and rushing faces.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What time of day is described in the poem?
questions.hint: Look for clues like “dawn”.
questions.explanation: References to dawn and the city waking up show early morning.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which words rhyme in verse 3?
questions.hint: Listen to the line endings.
questions.explanation: “Race”, “face” and “place” rhyme.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of this leaflet?
options: To persuade readers to join an outdoor club
To tell a story about a park
To give instructions for building a den
questions.hint: What does it want readers to do?
questions.explanation: It persuades readers to spend less time on screens and join the Saturday Explorers Club.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which persuasive technique is used in “Wouldn’t you like to feel calmer and sharper in class?”
questions.hint: It is a question that does not expect an answer.
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question makes the reader think and agree.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why does the writer use a statistic in the first paragraph?
options: To make the problem seem real and serious
questions.hint: Facts and figures can be convincing.
questions.explanation: The figure (more than five hours a day) makes the problem seem factual and urgent.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How much does the Saturday Explorers Club cost?
questions.hint: Paragraph 3.
questions.explanation: “The club is completely free.”

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Who is the leaflet mainly written for?
questions.hint: Look at who is addressed as “you” and the examples used.
questions.explanation: It mentions eleven-year-olds and lessons, and addresses the reader directly as a pupil.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is closest in meaning to “discover” in the final paragraph?
questions.hint: dis- + cover.
questions.explanation: To discover is to find out.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is a noun? “The brave knight rode quickly.”
questions.hint: A noun names a person, place or thing.
questions.explanation: “Knight” names a person.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Choose the correct verb: “Yesterday, we ___ to the museum.”

mistakes.3: Present tense — “yesterday” needs the past tense

questions.hint: Yesterday = past tense.
questions.explanation: “Went” is the past tense of “go”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the same tense throughout?
options: She opened the door and walked inside.
She opened the door and walks inside.
She will open the door and walked inside.
She opens the door and walked inside.
questions.hint: Both verbs should be in the past.
questions.explanation: “Opened” and “walked” are both past tense.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Rewrite in the active voice: “The cake was eaten by the children.”
options: The children were eaten by the cake.
questions.hint: Start with who did the action.
questions.explanation: Active voice: subject (the children) + verb (ate) + object (the cake).

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options: The boy and his dog ran.
The boy who lives next door has a dog.
questions.hint: Look for who, which, that, whose.
questions.explanation: “who lives next door” is a relative clause giving more information about the boy.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is a preposition in: “The keys are under the mat.”?
questions.hint: It shows position.
questions.explanation: “Under” shows where the keys are.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses “fewer” or “less” correctly?
options: There are less apples in the bowl today.
There are fewer apples in the bowl today.
She has less friends than me.
I have fewer water than you.
questions.hint: Use “fewer” for things you can count.
questions.explanation: Apples can be counted, so “fewer” is correct.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which is a modal verb showing possibility? “It ___ rain later.”
questions.hint: Modal verbs: can, could, may, might, should …
questions.explanation: “Might” shows possibility.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
options: I bought, apples bananas pears and grapes.
I, bought apples bananas pears and grapes.
I bought apples, bananas, pears and grapes.
I bought apples bananas, pears, and, grapes.
questions.hint: Commas separate items in a list.
questions.explanation: Commas go between list items; usually no comma before “and” in British English.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which shows the correct use of a contraction?
questions.hint: They’re = they are.
questions.explanation: “They’re” is short for “they are”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Where should the colon go? “You will need three things a pencil, a ruler and an eraser.”
questions.hint: A colon introduces a list.
questions.explanation: “You will need three things: a pencil, a ruler and an eraser.”

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses brackets correctly?
options: Mount Everest the world’s highest mountain (is in the Himalayas.
Mount (Everest the world’s highest) mountain is in the Himalayas.
Mount Everest (the world’s highest mountain) is in the Himalayas.
(Mount Everest the world’s) highest mountain is in the Himalayas.
questions.hint: Brackets hold extra information that could be removed.
questions.explanation: The bracketed words add information; the sentence makes sense without them.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: It was late we; decided to go home.
It was; late we decided to go home.
It; was late we decided to go home.
It was late; we decided to go home.
questions.hint: A semicolon joins two closely related complete sentences.
questions.explanation: Both “It was late” and “we decided to go home” are complete clauses.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is spelt correctly?
questions.hint: One collar, two sleeves: one c, two s.
questions.explanation: “Necessary” has one c and two s’s.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly for more than one owner?
options: The girls’ changing room was locked.
The girls’s changing room was locked.
The girl’s’ changing room was locked.
The girls changing’ room was locked.
questions.hint: For a plural ending in s, add the apostrophe after the s.
questions.explanation: “Girls’” shows the room belongs to several girls.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is spelt correctly?
questions.hint: There is “a rat” in it.
questions.explanation: Sep-a-rate: “separate”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which is a complex sentence?
options: When the bell rang, everyone hurried outside.
The bell rang and everyone hurried outside.
questions.hint: A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause.
questions.explanation: “When the bell rang” is a subordinate clause attached to the main clause.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word best fills the gap to show contrast? “The test was difficult; ___, most pupils passed.”

mistakes.2: “Therefore” shows a result, not a contrast

questions.hint: The second part is surprising given the first.
questions.explanation: “However” signals a contrast.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which is the best opening for a new paragraph about a change of time?
questions.hint: Paragraphs can start with a time adverbial.
questions.explanation: “Later that afternoon” clearly signals a time change.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is the clearest and most precise?
options: The runner was really really tired and fell at the end.
The runner did a thing at the end.
The exhausted runner collapsed across the finish line.
The tired runner who was tired fell over the line.
questions.hint: Look for precise vocabulary and no repetition.
questions.explanation: Precise words (“exhausted”, “collapsed”) say more in fewer words.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence has been edited correctly? “the children was playing football when it started to rain”
options: The children were playing football when it started to rain.
The Children were playing Football when it started to rain.
The children was playing football when it started to rain.
the children were playing football, when it started to rain
questions.hint: Capital letter, verb agreement, full stop.
questions.explanation: “Children” is plural, so “were”; start with a capital and end with a full stop.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which pair of sentences is joined correctly?
options: The film was long, it was exciting.
The film was long, but it was exciting.
The film was long it was exciting.
The film was long but, it was exciting.
questions.hint: Use a conjunction with the comma.
questions.explanation: A comma plus a conjunction (“but”) joins two main clauses.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is the best cohesive device to add an idea? “Bikes are good exercise. ___, they do not pollute the air.”
questions.hint: You are adding a second reason.
questions.explanation: “Furthermore” adds another point in the same direction.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is an antonym (opposite) of “ancient”?
questions.hint: Opposite of very old.
questions.explanation: “Modern” means new or recent.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which suffix turns “enjoy” into a noun?
questions.hint: enjoy + ? = a noun
questions.explanation: enjoy + ment = enjoyment.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is the most precise synonym for “walked” in: “The tired soldier ___ slowly home.”?
questions.hint: Think about how a tired person walks.
questions.explanation: “Trudged” means walked slowly and heavily.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: “The scientist was meticulous, checking every measurement three times.” What does “meticulous” mean?
questions.hint: Use the clue in the rest of the sentence.
questions.explanation: Checking everything three times shows great care — “meticulous”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does the root “aqua” mean in “aquarium” and “aquatic”?
questions.hint: Think about what an aquarium holds.
questions.explanation: “Aqua” comes from the Latin for water.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What is the name of the thin roots that poke out of the mud?
questions.hint: Paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 names them pneumatophores.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Give two ways mangroves protect people, according to paragraph 4.
options: They trap mud and stop coastlines washing away
questions.hint: Select both correct answers.
questions.explanation: Roots slow waves and trap mud, reducing storm damage and erosion.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why does the writer call mangrove forests “nurseries for the sea”?
options: The forests are full of schools
The sea is very young there
Young sea creatures grow up safely among the roots
questions.hint: What is a nursery for?
questions.explanation: Like a nursery for children, mangroves shelter young fish, crabs and shrimps while they grow.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 1, what does “remarkable” mean?
questions.hint: Worth remarking on.
questions.explanation: “Remarkable” means unusual or extraordinary.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How is the final paragraph different in tone from paragraph 4?
options: It is angry, while paragraph 4 is calm
It is hopeful, while paragraph 4 ends with a problem
It is funny, while paragraph 4 is serious
questions.hint: Compare the last sentence of each paragraph.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 ends with loss of mangroves; the final paragraph talks of replanting and “a small promise”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why do you think the writer put “breathe” in inverted commas in paragraph 2?
options: Because trees do not breathe exactly like animals do
questions.hint: Is the word being used in a special way?
questions.explanation: The inverted commas show the word is used loosely — the roots let the tree take in air, which is not quite the same as breathing.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How many times had Leila practised the piece?
questions.hint: Paragraph 1.
questions.explanation: One hundred and twelve times.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why is paragraph 2 only one sentence long?
options: To describe the hall in detail
Because the writer ran out of ideas
To emphasise the sudden shock of forgetting
questions.hint: How does a very short paragraph affect the reader?
questions.explanation: A single-sentence paragraph stands out, highlighting Leila’s sudden panic.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does “her fingers felt as though they belonged to someone else” suggest?
options: She was so nervous she felt she could not control her hands
questions.hint: How does fear affect the body?
questions.explanation: Nerves made her feel disconnected from her own hands.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What helped Leila remember the music?
options: She read the music from a sheet
The judge played the first note
Thinking about home, her practice and her brother
She left the hall and came back
questions.hint: Paragraph 4.
questions.explanation: She closed her eyes and thought of her bedroom, tally marks and brother — familiar, calming memories.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which technique is used in “like water from a tap that had been stuck for years”?
questions.hint: Look for “like”.
questions.explanation: It compares the music to water using “like” — a simile.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does the ending suggest about Leila’s performance?
options: It was very good and moved the judge
The judges did not hear it
questions.hint: Why might a judge clap quietly after silence?
questions.explanation: The silence followed by the judge clapping suggests the performance impressed and moved her.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In which year was the wooden “running machine” built?
questions.hint: Paragraph 1.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why were penny-farthings dangerous?
options: Riders could be thrown over the handlebars if they hit a stone
questions.hint: Paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: Hitting a stone could throw the rider head-first over the handlebars.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How is this text mainly organised?
options: As an argument for and against
questions.hint: Look at the dates and time words.
questions.explanation: It moves from 1817 to the 1860s, 1880s and today — chronological order.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why did cycling become popular with “ordinary people”?
options: Safer bicycles let them travel further without needing a horse
questions.hint: Paragraphs 3 and 4.
questions.explanation: The safer, more comfortable design meant ordinary people could travel several kilometres cheaply.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: In paragraph 5, what does “instantly” mean?
questions.hint: In an instant.
questions.explanation: “Instantly” means at once.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: When does the market appear?
options: On the first foggy morning of autumn
questions.hint: Paragraph 1.
questions.explanation: “On the first foggy morning of autumn.”

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does paragraph 2 tell us about Ben’s attitude before he visits?
options: He was doubtful and did not believe the stories
He was terrified of the market
He wanted to buy a clock
questions.hint: “He had never believed a word.”
questions.explanation: He had heard the stories but did not believe them — he was sceptical.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: What does the description of the stallholder’s coat suggest about her?
options: She is mysterious and may have travelled to many places
questions.hint: Maps are linked with journeys.
questions.explanation: A coat stitched from maps hints at travel and mystery, fitting the magical market.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Why do you think Ben decided not to buy a memory and went to find his sister instead?
options: He did not have any money
He realised he could make real good memories with the people he loves
questions.hint: He had a coin. What did he choose to do instead?
questions.explanation: He had the coin but chose to go home to his sister — suggesting real memories with family matter more.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: How does the opening paragraph hook the reader?
options: It lists the prices at the market
It describes a mysterious market that appears without anyone seeing it arrive
questions.hint: What makes you want to read on?
questions.explanation: A market that appears from nowhere creates mystery and curiosity.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is an adjective? “The enormous whale swam slowly.”
questions.hint: Adjectives describe nouns.
questions.explanation: “Enormous” describes the whale.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is in the future tense?
options: We visit our cousins every week.
We will visit our cousins next week.
We are visiting our cousins now.
We visited our cousins last week.
questions.hint: Look for “will”.
questions.explanation: “Will visit” refers to the future.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Neither of the boys are ready.
Neither of the boys were ready.
Neither of the boys was ready.
Neither of the boys be ready.
questions.hint: “Neither” is singular.
questions.explanation: “Neither” takes a singular verb: “was”.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: “Look out!” shouted Mum. “There’s a car coming.”
Look out! “shouted Mum” There’s a car coming.
“Look out! shouted Mum.” There’s a car coming.
“Look out” shouted Mum! “There’s a car coming”
questions.hint: Spoken words and their punctuation go inside speech marks.
questions.explanation: Each piece of speech is inside its own speech marks with its punctuation.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a dash correctly?
options: I opened the box it was — empty.
I — opened the box it was empty.
I opened the box — it was empty.
I opened — the box it was empty.
questions.hint: A dash can show a pause before extra information.
questions.explanation: The dash separates two related clauses for dramatic effect.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which word is spelt correctly?
questions.hint: It contains the word “finite”.
questions.explanation: De-finite-ly.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which is the best way to combine: “The fox was hungry. The fox crept towards the henhouse.”?
options: The fox was hungry and the fox crept towards the henhouse.
The hungry fox crept towards the henhouse.
The fox was hungry, the fox crept towards the henhouse.
Hungry, the fox was hungry and crept.
questions.hint: Avoid repeating “the fox”.
questions.explanation: Using “hungry” as an adjective combines the ideas without repetition.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a fronted adverbial with correct punctuation?
options: Without a sound, the cat leapt onto the wall.
The cat leapt, without a sound onto the wall.
Without, a sound the cat leapt onto the wall.
Without a sound the cat, leapt onto the wall.
questions.hint: A comma follows the fronted adverbial.
questions.explanation: “Without a sound,” is fronted and followed by a comma.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which prefix means “not” in “impossible”?
questions.hint: Look at the beginning.
questions.explanation: “im-” means not: not possible.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: “After the long drought, the river was barely a trickle.” What does “drought” mean?
options: a long period with little or no rain
questions.hint: The river was nearly empty.
questions.explanation: A drought is a long time with very little rain.

questions.subject: english
questions.prompt: Which sentence contains a subordinate clause beginning with a conjunction?
options: Mia was tired and finished her homework.
Although she was tired, Mia finished her homework.
questions.hint: Subordinating conjunctions: although, because, when, if …
questions.explanation: “Although she was tired” is a subordinate clause.
